sourceNote: Selective DGT editorial notes. UBS5/NA28 comparisons are based on the SBLGNT apparatus; UBS5 and NA28 share the same base text in John.

1:14: John says the Word “became flesh” (σὰρξ ἐγένετο), a deliberately concrete expression for entering human existence.
1:18: μονογενὴς θεός is unusually compact. DGT treats μονογενής as “unique/only” rather than deriving its sense from the verb “beget.”
1:34: SBLGNT reads ὁ ἐκλεκτός, “the Chosen One,” while UBS5/NA28 reads ὁ υἱός, “the Son.” This is one of John’s clearest differences between the two modern critical texts.
2:4: τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί is a Semitic-style idiom, literally close to “what to me and to you?” English translations must supply the relationship implied by context.
3:3: ἄνωθεν can mean either “again” or “from above.” Nicodemus hears the first sense; Jesus’ wording permits the second, which drives the exchange.
3:8: πνεῦμα can mean “wind” or “spirit,” and πνεῖ means “blows.” The Greek wordplay links the wind’s unseen movement with birth from the Spirit.
5:2: SBLGNT reads Βηθεσδά (Bethesda); UBS5/NA28 reads Βηθζαθά (Bethzatha). The difference is the place-name form, not the event being described.
6:54: John shifts here to τρώγω, a more concrete verb for eating, after previously using forms of ἐσθίω/φάγω. English often obscures the change.
8:58: γενέσθαι (“came to be”) is contrasted with ἐγώ εἰμι (“I am”), producing the striking wording, “before Abraham came to be, I am.”
10:16: The Greek is μία ποίμνη, εἷς ποιμήν: “one flock, one shepherd.” It does not say “one fold.”
10:29: SBLGNT reads πάντων μεῖζων, naturally taking “my Father” as “greater than all.” UBS5/NA28 reads πάντων μεῖζόν, which can instead make what the Father has given Jesus the thing “greater than all.”
14:2: μοναί means “dwelling places” or “rooms.” The traditional “mansions” comes from an older English sense of a dwelling, not from a Greek word meaning large houses.
14:7: SBLGNT and UBS5/NA28 differ noticeably here. SBLGNT has the past-looking “if you had known me, you would have known my Father also,” while UBS5/NA28 uses forms that can be rendered “if you have known me, you will know my Father also.”
14:16: παράκλητος is difficult to compress into one English word: advocate, helper, counselor, or one called alongside are all aspects of the term.
15:2: αἴρει can mean “takes away/removes” and in other contexts “lifts up.” In this vine image DGT follows the ordinary pruning contrast: fruitless branches are removed, fruitful ones are pruned.
19:30: τετέλεσται is perfect tense: not merely “it ended,” but “it has been completed/accomplished.”
20:17: μὴ μου ἅπτου is better understood as “do not hold on to me” or “stop clinging to me” than as a prohibition against any momentary touch.
20:31: SBLGNT reads πιστεύητε, naturally “that you may continue believing,” while UBS5/NA28 reads πιστεύσητε, which more readily allows “that you may come to believe.” The difference can affect how John’s stated purpose is understood.
21:15: John varies ἀγαπάω and φιλέω in Jesus’ exchange with Peter. The verbs can overlap substantially in Koine Greek, so the passage should not be made to depend on two sharply different kinds of love.
